html:
The Luiseño, who call themselves Payómkawichum, are an Indigenous people of the coast and hills of southern California, between today's Los Angeles and San Diego counties. They speak a Uto-Aztecan language and lived on acorns, seeds, game and seafood.

Their religion centred on Chinigchinich, a teacher god, and on initiation rites for boys that used the drug toloache (datura), along with ground paintings of the world. The Spanish name comes from the mission of San Luis Rey, founded among them in 1798, one of the Spanish missions in California. Mission life, disease and then American settlement took most of their land. Today several Luiseño bands hold small reservations. See Payómkawichum and their neighbours the Cahuilla and Tongva.
